# Audio direction — the Bonelight sound contract

Decided 2026-09-05, alongside the first complete SFX set. This file is to sound what
`.ai/art-direction.md` is to pixels: the format, the element palette, the mix, the frequency
budget, the engine settings, and the rules that keep seventy-one sounds behaving like one
system. Read it before adding, retuning or wiring any sound.

`.ai/audio-manifest.md` lists every file and where it is meant to be triggered. This file
says *why* each one sounds the way it does.

**The one-line version:** every sound is generated by code in `tools/audio/`, never recorded
or hand-edited; the first 8 ms of every element sound is the same white transient so a cast
always reads as "a spell went off"; and a sound's loudness is set by how *often* it plays,
not by how important it feels.

## 1. Why the set is synthesised

Three hard constraints, in the order they bind:

- This machine has **Python 2.7 with PIL and nothing else** — no numpy, no ffmpeg, no
  ImageMagick, no audio encoder, no virtualenv. `tools/art/` already works under exactly that
  constraint, and `tools/audio/` follows it.
- There is **no audio model in the loop**. Nothing in this pipeline can render a description
  into a recording. What it can do is oscillators, envelopes, filters and saturation, which
  is the sfxr/Bfxr vocabulary and a natural fit for a pixel-art roguelite.
- **No one working on this project can hear the files by reading the source.** That is why
  `tools/audio/analyse.py` exists and why section 8 is a measurement, not an assertion.

The consequence is a boundary worth stating plainly: this pipeline produces synthetic,
retro-adjacent sound. It cannot produce voice, foley or recorded impacts. This line used to say
it could not produce music either, and the two stock tracks were kept for that reason; both
were then removed for want of a licence, and the music is now generated too - section 11.

## 2. Format

| Property | Value | Why it is not negotiable |
|---|---|---|
| Channels | **mono** | `AudioStreamPlayer2D` will not pan a stereo stream, and nearly every gameplay sound in this game is positional. Stereo throws away the only spatial cue a top-down swarm has. |
| Sample rate | 44100 Hz | Godot's WAV importer resamples anything else. |
| Bit depth | 16-bit PCM | The importer's native format; no decode cost at play time. |
| Container | `.wav` | There is no OGG encoder on this machine. WAV is also the only format Godot will loop sample-accurately. |
| Location | `assets/sfx/`, flat | One directory, prefix-sorted names. No per-category subdirectories. |

Music differs on three rows - 22050 Hz, RMS rather than peak targets, no fades - and section 11
says why.
| Fades | 0.4 ms in, 6 ms out, applied **before** normalising | A buffer that starts or ends off zero is a click, and a click at swarm rates is a buzz. A fade applied *after* normalising attenuates the transient the mix target was measured against — that bug cost four sounds up to 9 dB of attack before it was caught. |

Loop sounds are the one exception: they are **not** faded, because on a loop the fade *is*
the click. See `spell_beam_loop` in `tools/audio/sfx.py` for how a seamless loop is built.

## 3. The pipeline

```
tools/audio/synth.py    oscillators, envelopes, filters, saturation, reverb, WAV writer
tools/audio/palette.py  the twelve element voices + the shared transient
tools/audio/sfx.py      one function per named sound, plus REGISTRY
tools/audio/build.py    writes assets/sfx/, reports levels, flags problems
tools/audio/analyse.py  the distinctness audit (section 8)
```

```
python tools/audio/build.py                 # write the whole set (about 90 s)
python tools/audio/build.py cast_ impact_   # only names containing these
python tools/audio/build.py --preview       # also write per-category audition reels
python tools/audio/build.py --manifest      # print the markdown table for the manifest doc
python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse     # the distinctness audit
```

**The generators are the source; the `.wav` files are output.** Never hand-edit a file in
`assets/sfx/` — edit the builder and re-run, exactly as with `tools/art/`. Every random draw
comes from a seeded `random.Random`, so a rebuild is byte-identical; if two runs differ,
something has introduced time- or address-dependent randomness and that is a bug.

`tools/audio/_preview_<category>.wav` are audition reels — every sound in a category with
250 ms gaps. They are working files: nothing loads them and they are not shipped.

## 4. The element palette

`.ai/art-direction.md` §3 states the visual rule for the twelve elements:

> The core of every element's effect is white-hot. Identity lives in the mid and edge.

This is the same rule in time:

> **The first 8 ms of every element sound is the same white transient. Identity lives in the
> body and the tail.**

So a cast reads as "a spell went off" on the attack, and *which* element answers a beat
later. The transient is the audio equivalent of the reserved rim colour: shared, bright, and
never element-tinted. One drawn burst serves every element by remapping its ramp; one
transient serves every element by prefixing its body.

"White" means shared and untinted, not unbounded. Until 2026-10-15 the transient was noise
highpassed at 2.6 kHz with nothing above it, so all twenty-four element files opened on a burst
of 10-20 kHz hiss; it is now band-limited to 1.6-5.5 kHz. See section 6, "The ceiling".

The numbers live in `ELEMENTS` in `tools/audio/palette.py` — that dict is the source of
truth and this table is its description. Rows are ordered to match the colour table in the
art contract. Centroid is measured by `analyse.py`, not authored, and is the cast's after the
2026-10-15 softening pass (section 6, "The ceiling"); the old figure is kept for the record.

| Element | Character | Body | Centroid (was) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire | roaring, gritty, low | irregularly gated bandpassed noise sweeping 1400→200 Hz over a sine thump, heavily saturated | 2.3 kHz (3.9) |
| Ice | brittle, glassy, high | inharmonic partials (1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.93) on 1050→1220 Hz, plus a frost hiss at 3→4.2 kHz | 2.8 kHz (6.7) |
| Arcane | shimmering, tonal, rising | two triangles detuned 0.7%, tremolo at 17 Hz, filter opening 2000→4000 Hz | 1.5 kHz (5.8) |
| Darkness | swelling, sub-heavy, airless | a saw + almost no noise, built forwards then **reversed** so it arrives instead of decaying | 0.6 kHz (4.0) |
| Light | bell, sustained, warm-bright | a struck bell stack on G5 (was A5) with a fifth over it | 1.6 kHz (5.3) |
| Grass | woody, short, blunt | a filtered saw pluck with a pitched-noise knock | 1.6 kHz (2.5) |
| Earth | low thud, rubble | a sine dropping 150→44 Hz plus decimated lowpassed noise | 0.6 kHz (2.1) |
| Wind | airy, pitchless, no bass | two bandpasses sweeping in opposite directions, highpassed at 520 Hz, topping out near 2.8 kHz | 3.2 kHz (6.7) |
| Lightning | fast, bright, crackling | a 3800→900 Hz noise zap plus irregularly gated 2.4-5.5 kHz noise | 4.7 kHz (10.8) |
| Poison | wet, bubbling, mid-band | 9 Hz FM gurgle through a narrow bandpass, with gated blips | 1.2 kHz (4.4) |
| Metal | struck, ringing, inharmonic | six inharmonic partials (1 : 1.71 : 2.46 : 3.39 : 4.51 : 5.88), on 520 Hz, ring-modulated at 137 Hz | 1.2 kHz (3.6) |
| Water | droplet, dark wash | a fast rising droplet over a heavily lowpassed wash held at 0.34 gain | 1.1 kHz (5.6) |

Each element ships two files: `cast_<element>.wav` and `impact_<element>.wav`.

**The impact is not a quieter cast.** Impacts fire far more often — one cast can produce a
dozen — so `palette.impact()` squeezes the body to 55%, adds a low thump, cuts the reverb to
60%, sits under a lower ceiling (5.2 kHz against the cast's 7), and lands 4 dB under the cast. Darkness additionally plays *forwards* at impact length:
the reversal is a cast gesture, and an impact has already arrived.

**A new element means a new row in `ELEMENTS`, reviewed, then used.** Never numbers typed
inline at a call site. That is the same budget discipline the colour table is under, and for
the same reason: twelve is already at the edge of what a player can tell apart.

## 5. Loudness is a function of frequency of play

This is the rule the whole mix hangs off, and it is counterintuitive:

> **How loud a sound is depends on how often it plays, not on how important the event is.**

An XP orb is a genuinely important event and it is the quietest file in the game, because a
run collects thousands of them. A boss death is the loudest, because it happens once.

Targets are peak dBFS, set per entry in `REGISTRY` in `tools/audio/sfx.py`. `build.py`
normalises every file to its target, so **the registry *is* the mix**: the game plays these
at unity and balance is changed by editing one number and re-running, not by hunting
`VolumeDb` overrides across forty call sites.

| Band | Peak target | Typical members |
|---|---|---|
| Once a run | −3 to −5 dBFS | `boss_death`, `player_death`, `stage_clear`, `meta_unlock`, `spell_evolve`, `level_up` |
| Once a minute | −6 to −9 dBFS | `chest_open`, `player_hurt`, `elite_spawn`, `spell_explosion`, `card_select` |
| Once a second | −11 to −15 dBFS | casts (−11), `enemy_death_*`, `enemy_shoot`, most of `ui_*` |
| Many times a second | −15 to −23 dBFS | `impact_*` (−15), `enemy_hurt_*` (−19), `spell_orbit` (−22), `pickup_xp` (−23) |
| Subliminal | −26 dBFS | `ui_hover` — it plays on every mouse movement across a button |

`pickup_xp` sits 20 dB under `boss_death`. That gap is deliberate and it is what stops a
level-3 Arcane build from turning into white noise.

Casts were at −9 and impacts at −13 until 2026-10-15, both above their own rows. They came
down to the table when the persistent emitters (Solar Flare, Toxic Spore Burst, Cinderbreath)
started cueing every pulse, which put more casts in a minute than the table was drawn for.

## 6. The frequency budget

Only one thing may own each band at a time, or a dense screen turns to mud:

- **Sub, below 80 Hz** — `spell_explosion`, `boss_death`, `boss_roar`, `earth`. Nothing else
  may put energy here. A swarm sound with a sub component is the fastest way to lose the mix.
- **Low, 80–300 Hz** — `player_hurt`, `enemy_death_heavy`, the thumps under impacts.
- **Mid, 300 Hz–2 kHz** — the music lives here. Gameplay sounds cross it briefly and leave.
- **High-mid, 2–8 kHz** — where most element identity sits, and where the ear is most
  sensitive. The most contested band in the game; check anything new against a busy screen.
- **Top, above 5 kHz** — effectively nobody. It used to be "cheap to occupy because the music
  barely reaches it", and that is exactly how the set drifted shrill: see the ceiling below.

### The ceiling - nothing that repeats lives up there (2026-10-15)

The complaint was "many noises are high pitched and annoying", and `analyse.py` agreed: the
`hf` column (share of spectral magnitude above 4 kHz) had `cast_lightning` at 90%, every UI tick
at 72-77%, `cast_ice` at 60% and the median element file near 30%. Almost none of that was
identity. It was three constructs, each repeated hundreds of times a minute:

- **An open highpass on noise.** The shared transient, the UI `_tick`, the lightning crackle and
  the bow snap were all "noise, highpassed at 1.4-5 kHz" with nothing above, which is a hiss to
  Nyquist. Every one is now a band: a highpass *and* a lowpass.
- **Saturation without a filter after it.** `drive()` adds odd harmonics far above the source.
  The element bodies, `enemy_hurt_*` and the beam now pass a lowpass after the drive.
- **Raw pitch too high for the rate it plays at.** `pickup_xp` was a 1050-1580 Hz sine pitched up
  to 1.5x by the streak ladder; it is now 760-1140 Hz with the ladder capped at 1.4x. Light's bell
  moved from A5 to G5, ice and metal down by about a sixth, lightning's zap from 6.2 to 3.8 kHz.

**The rule.** Every element file passes `palette.CAST_CEILING` (7 kHz) or `IMPACT_CEILING`
(5.2 kHz) before its tail. Anything that can fire more than once a second keeps its `hf` under
about 15%; lightning is the one exception, because brightness *is* its identity, and it is still
the brightest thing in the set at 39-55% rather than 90%. A rare, one-off UI flourish
(`card_appear`, three per level-up) may sit higher if lowering it collides with a neighbour - but
it is lowpassed, not left open. Check a new sound's `hf` column before shipping it, the same way
its confusion distance is checked.

| Sound | Plays | Centroid before | after | hf before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cast_lightning` / `impact_lightning` | per chain | 10.8 / 10.3 kHz | 4.7 / 3.7 kHz | 90 / 86% | 55 / 39% |
| `cast_ice` / `impact_ice` | per cast | 6.7 / 5.6 kHz | 2.8 / 2.0 kHz | 60 / 50% | 22 / 12% |
| `cast_wind` / `impact_wind` | per cast | 6.7 / 5.4 kHz | 3.2 / 2.0 kHz | 52 / 42% | 25 / 13% |
| `cast_light` | every Solar Flare pulse | 5.3 kHz | 1.6 kHz | 32% | 6% |
| `cast_arcane` | per cast | 5.8 kHz | 1.5 kHz | 37% | 6% |
| `enemy_hurt_*` | dozens a second | 3.3-3.5 kHz | 1.3-1.4 kHz | 27-29% | 6-7% |
| `ui_hover` / `ui_click` / `ui_back` | every button | 9.9-10.2 kHz | 1.8-2.4 kHz | 72-73% | 12-16% |
| `reroll` | per reroll | 10.4 kHz | 2.5 kHz | 77% | 17% |
| `spell_orbit` | on a timer, all run | 5.0 kHz | 2.4 kHz | 43% | 13% |
| `enemy_shoot` | per ranged shot | 6.5 kHz | 2.3 kHz | 51% | 15% |
| `spell_bow_release` | per arrow | 9.4 kHz | 3.4 kHz | 71% | 31% |
| `player_shield_break` | per break | 8.5 kHz | 3.8 kHz | 71% | 32% |
| `pickup_xp` | thousands a run | 1.3 kHz | 1.0 kHz | 0% | 0% |

## 7. Variation at play time, not on disk

Repetition fatigue is solved in the engine, not by generating more files:

- **Pitch.** Randomise `AudioStreamPlayer2D.PitchScale` in roughly `0.94–1.06` on every
  frequently-repeating one-shot. `pickup_xp` should additionally ramp its pitch **upward**
  with the collection streak and reset when the streak breaks — one file, an entire ladder.
- **Variants.** Only three sounds ship variants (`enemy_hurt_a/b/c`), because only they
  repeat fast enough to machine-gun. They differ by seed and by a few Hz, never by intent;
  the audit declares them as twins rather than flagging them.
- **Rate limiting.** `enemy_hurt_*` and `impact_*` must be throttled at the call site — one
  per ~60 ms across all enemies, not one per hit. An AoE landing on forty enemies must play
  one impact, not forty.
- **Voice cap.** Godot has a global limit on simultaneous streams; hitting it drops sounds
  arbitrarily, including important ones. Cap the swarm-rate categories yourself so the
  budget is spent on things the player needs to hear.

## 8. The audit — measure distinctness, do not assert it

`.ai/art-direction.md` §4 does not claim the enemy silhouettes are distinct; it measures the
overlap and reports 1.00 for the two that are the same sprite. `tools/audio/analyse.py` is
that audit for sound:

```
python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse
```

It reports spectral centroid, 85% rolloff, spread, attack time and crest factor for every
sound, then the pairwise cosine distance between **profiles** — 24 log-spaced spectral bands
plus 12 envelope bands. The envelope half is load-bearing: on spectrum alone, `reroll`
measured as a near-twin of `ui_click`, which it literally is — five copies of it spread over
200 ms. Shape over time is to sound what silhouette is to a sprite.

**Anything at or below 0.10 is confusable and must be fixed or declared.** The current set
measures **0 confusable pairs**, with the three declared twins listed in `TWINS`. Nine real
collisions were found and fixed on the way there, and they are the useful part of the
record because they are the mistakes this palette invites. The last three surfaced only
once the envelope term was added to the metric, which is itself the argument for having it.

| Pair | Was | Why it collided | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cast_arcane` / `cast_water` | 0.041 | both mid-band tonal sweeps over a noise bed | arcane moved up an octave; water’s wash cut to 0.34 gain and the droplet made dominant |
| `cast_fire` / `cast_wind` | 0.058 | both are just wide-band noise under an envelope | fire pushed down to 1400→200 Hz with a stronger thump; wind highpassed at 520 Hz, because air has no bass |
| `stage_clear` / `meta_unlock` | 0.029 | two ascending bell arpeggios in one register | `meta_unlock` rebuilt as a sustained stacked-fifths swell — a swelling chord against a struck one |
| `elite_spawn` / `boss_roar` | 0.082 | an elite shared a boss’s register | `elite_spawn` rebuilt as a reversed struck-metal tone an octave and a half up |
| `card_appear` / `ui_open` | 0.039 | both whoosh-plus-bell, played 400 ms apart | `card_appear` stripped to a pure high-band paper flick with no pitched component |
| `chest_open` / `pickup_health` | 0.094 | every reward in the game was a bell | `pickup_health` rebuilt as a soft filtered sine glow, so HP owns its own timbre |
| `impact_darkness` / `impact_wind` | 0.092 | reversing a swell and then applying `impact()`’s decay leaves a shapeless blob | darkness plays **forwards** below 0.4 s — the reversal is a cast gesture, and an impact has already arrived |
| `pickup_health` / `pickup_magnet` | 0.078 | two smooth rising tonal glides | `pickup_magnet` rebuilt as six accelerating blips, because the event is many orbs arriving |
| `level_up` / `spell_evolve` | 0.089 | both led with the same bell arpeggio, and they fire seconds apart | `spell_evolve` reordered swell-first, bells last — a transformation with a result, not a second level |
| `cast_arcane` / `cast_light` | 0.100 | softening pass: light dropped to E5, into the register arcane sweeps through | light settled on G5 and arcane's filter kept opening to 4 kHz |
| `spell_beam_start` / `spell_bow_draw` | 0.071 | softening pass: a 4.5 kHz lowpass made the ignition another rising band like the creak | ignition lowpassed at 6.5 kHz (it plays once per beam), and the creak moved down to 620-1300 Hz |
| `spell_orbit` / `spell_bow_release` | 0.075 | softening pass: both became a mid-band swipe | the orbit leans on its 820 Hz ring - a tone is what the bow lacks |
| `card_appear` / `ui_close` | 0.079 | softening pass: the paper flick lowered into the close whoosh | the flick kept its 1.8-4.6 kHz band and is lowpassed at 7 kHz instead |

The lesson generalises: **collisions happen between sounds built from the same construct**,
and the fix is almost always to change the construct rather than to nudge a frequency.

## 8b. The mix audit - what forty of them at once sounds like

`analyse.py` answers "can these two sounds be told apart". It cannot answer the question that
decides whether a game sounds good: **when forty of them fire at once, can you still hear the
one that matters.** `tools/audio/mixsim.py` answers that one.

```
python tools/audio/mixsim.py                     # every scenario, both policies
python tools/audio/mixsim.py --scenario lategame # the worst case
```

It replays a synthetic minute of a run - hit rates ramping with wave pressure, spells on their
cooldowns, a boss roar partway through - through a model of `SfxPlayer`, mixes the result,
writes a `.wav` you can listen to, and reports peak, crest factor, clipping, and the number the
exercise exists for: **headroom**, per critical event, meaning how far that boss roar rose above
the swarm already playing. Below about 6 dB a sound is present but not noticed; below 3 dB it
may as well not have played.

**The model is parsed, not copied.** Voice counts and throttle windows are read out of
`scripts/SfxPlayer.cs` at run time, and the simulator refuses to start if a constant it expects
has been renamed. A simulator that quietly stops matching the runtime is worse than none,
because it launders a guess into a measurement.

It approximates Godot 2D attenuation as `(1 - d/max)` and does not model the music bus, reverb
interaction between voices, or the listener. Good enough to rank two policies against each
other; not a mastering tool.

### What the first run found

| Finding | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **The mix clips in every scenario, including the sparse early game** | peak +1.5 to +2.5 dBFS, 81-234 clipped samples | The registry levels were each set in isolation and nothing had measured their sum. A limiter at -1 dBFS fixes it for 2.5 dB of crest factor. |
| **A tiered priority policy is worth 5-8 dB** on critical sounds | worst critical headroom +3.6 dB to +12.1 dB; voice steals 215 to 35 in the late game | Validated in simulation, not yet implemented. |
| **`elite_spawn` cannot cut through a late-game swarm** | -20.5 dB under the swarm, still -10.3 dB after ducking and ignoring distance | Not a mix problem. It is a rising swell, and a swell has no transient to punch through noise with. It needs redrawing in `sfx.py`, not more gain. |
| Throttling already discards a third of all events | 1954 of 5107 suppressed in the late game | Existing behaviour, now visible. |

The third row is the useful shape of this tool: it turns "that does not cut through" from an
opinion into a number, and points at the generator rather than the mixer.

## 8c. Priority and ducking

Two axes that feel like one knob and are not. Conflating them is the mistake this section
exists to prevent.

- **Priority** decides who wins when voices run out. Every sound has one.
- **Duck authority** decides who makes other sounds quieter. Almost nothing has it.

`SfxCatalog.SfxTier` declares three tiers, and `RegressionChecks` warns if more than fourteen
sounds are Critical, because the mechanism only works while Critical is rare.

| Tier | Members | When voices run out | Distance | Ducks others |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Swarm` | `enemy_hurt_*`, all `impact_*`, `pickup_xp`, `spell_orbit` | **drops itself** - never steals | attenuated | no |
| `Normal` | casts, enemy deaths, UI, pickups, chest | steals a Swarm voice, else drops | attenuated | no |
| `Critical` | the ten rare, run-defining sounds | steals Swarm then Normal; never stolen | **ignored** | yes |

**`player_hurt` is not Critical**, despite being loud and important. While the player is being
swarmed it fires several times a second, and a duck that retriggers before it releases turns
the mix into a pump and removes hit feedback at the exact moment the player is dying.

**Criticals ignore distance attenuation.** `mixsim` measured `elite_spawn` at 20 dB *under* the
swarm purely because it happened to spawn across the screen. A rule that says "this is the
sound that matters" and then halves it for being 380 px away is not a rule. They keep their
position, so they still pan.

### The bus tree

```
Master
├── Music
└── SFX            <- the player volume slider, plus one AudioEffectHardLimiter at -1 dBFS
    ├── SFX_Bed       <- everything Normal and Swarm; this is the bus the duck lowers
    └── SFX_Priority  <- Critical only; never ducked
```

The split exists so the duck can never fight the volume slider. If both lived on one bus, the
duck would overwrite whatever the player had just set - and a critical sound would duck itself.

The duck is **scripted, not sidechained**. Godot does have `AudioEffectCompressor.Sidechain`
and it would sound more organic, but a fixed curve is exactly reproducible inside
`tools/audio/mixsim.py` and a compressor is not. While nobody on this project can hear the
difference to referee it, predictable beats organic.

`DuckDb` is -6 dB and `DuckReleaseSeconds` is 0.30, both in `SfxPlayer` - and `mixsim` parses
them out of that file rather than keeping its own copy. It deliberately does not duck to
silence: losing hit feedback during a boss roar is worse than the noise it was fixing.

## 9. Godot integration

`.ai/audio-manifest.md` holds the wiring table and what remains. What exists now:

- **Buses.** `default_bus_layout.tres` defines Master, Music, SFX and SFX's two children
  (see the tree in section 8c), with an `AudioEffectHardLimiter` at -1 dBFS on SFX.
  `MusicPlayer` and `SfxPlayer` resolve every bus by name with a fallback one level up, and
  `RegressionChecks` warns for each missing bus and for a missing limiter - all three
  fallbacks are silent, and one of them was a shipped bug before the layout existed.
- **Positional vs global.** Anything with a world position — casts, impacts, enemy sounds —
  uses `AudioStreamPlayer2D`. UI, stingers and `player_*` use plain `AudioStreamPlayer`.
- **Import settings.** Godot's WAV importer defaults are correct for everything here, with
  one exception meant to be applied: a loop needs `edit/loop_mode=2`, which is **Forward** - the
  importer's enum is *Detect From WAV, Disabled, Forward, Ping-Pong, Backward*.
  `assets/sfx/spell_beam_loop.wav.import` carries `edit/loop_mode=1`, which this line used to
  call Forward and which is in fact **Disabled**: Godot 4.5 loads that file with `LoopMode` 0
  (checked 2026-10-20). The sound is not wired yet, so nothing is broken today, but it must be
  set to 2 before the beam plays it. The music in `assets/music/` carries 2 and
  `RegressionChecks.ValidateMusic` checks it. The setting lives in the `.import` file, not the
  WAV, so **regenerating the file keeps it but deleting the `.import` loses it**. Note also that the
  importer defaults to `compress/mode=2`, which is QOA — lossy. That is the right trade for
  short effects; if an artefact ever shows up on the quietest files, PCM is `compress/mode=0`.
- **`tools/audio/` carries a `.gdignore`.** Nothing in there is loaded by the game, and
  without it Godot imports several megabytes of audition reel into `.godot/`.
- **Preloading and pooling.** `SfxPlayer` loads all 71 streams in `_Ready` and plays them
  through a fixed pool of 24 positional and 8 non-positional voices. Never call
  `ResourceLoader.Load` or `new AudioStreamPlayer2D()` on a frame the game is running.
- **Persistence.** Volumes live in `SaveData` as linear 0..1 and are applied by
  `AudioSettings.ApplyFromSave` from `SfxPlayer._Ready`, which runs after `SaveManager`
  because of the autoload order in `project.godot`.

## 10. Adding a sound

1. Write a builder in `tools/audio/sfx.py`. Compose from `synth.py` primitives; if it is
   elemental, go through `palette.body()` rather than typing new numbers.
2. Add it to `REGISTRY` with a category, a peak target chosen from the table in §5, and the
   loop flag. **A function that is not in the registry does not ship** — `build.py` does not
   scan the module.
3. `python tools/audio/build.py <name>` and check the report: it must hit its target exactly,
   and must not be flagged as clipped, long or under target.
4. `python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse` and confirm it did not land within 0.10 of an
   existing sound in its category. If it did, change the construct, not the gain.
5. Add its row to `.ai/audio-manifest.md` with the intended trigger site.
6. Commit the generator change **and** the regenerated `.wav`.

## 11. Music

Added 2026-10-20 with one chapter, the Forest, which the menu and every chapter played. Rewritten
2026-10-22 as **a menu theme and nine chapter sets, every one of them faster and driven** (the
brief is below). Until 2026-10-20 the game had no music at all: the two stock tracks were removed
before the repo went public because neither licence could be shown (`.ai/asset-licensing.md`).
The music is generated by the same pipeline as the effects, under the same rules, and is ours
outright.

```
python tools/audio/music.py                          # render every piece into assets/music/
python tools/audio/music.py cave --scratch           # render one to tools/audio/_music_preview/
python tools/audio/music.py cave --scratch --balance # ...and print how loud each voice is in each stem
python tools/audio/music.py --report [--scratch]     # seam, loudness and size of what is on disk
python tools/audio/music.py --journey [--scratch]    # audition reels: one per chapter, the menu, a sampler
python tools/audio/analyse.py --music [--scratch]    # where each stem's energy sits in the budget
python tools/audio/mixsim.py --music --policy tiered [--scratch] [--sets cave,swamp]
                                                     # the effects with each chapter's music under them
```

A piece takes one to two minutes to render. **Render one at a time** - the machine is shared, and
nine in parallel starve everything else on it.

### The brief: action, not ambience (2026-10-22)

The request was *"the music should change from the main menu to music that is specific to every
stage, and feels more action packed."* The Forest it replaced was a dark 6/8 at 64 - a walk - and
it was all there was. What changed:

- **Every chapter has its own set, and the menu its own theme.** The theme is the only slow thing
  left (72), so the moment a run starts is audibly a change of gear.
- **Tempo.** 104 to 168 to the counted beat - the dotted quarter in 6/8, the eighth in the swamp's
  7/8 - against the old 64.
- **Every stem moves.** The bed is no longer pads alone: it carries an ostinato under its chords -
  spiccato strings in six chapters, a reed organ pumping each group in the swamp, an oud riff in
  the sands, pizzicato oom-pah-pah in the Sketchbook - so the opening seconds of a run, bed only
  until 28 enemies are alive, are already going somewhere. The pulse is drums, a driving bass and
  usually an arpeggio. The lead is a hook built on a rhythm that comes back every bar (the
  dungeon's "da-da DUM", the forest's quarter-eighth gallop), stated in A and answered in B.
- **Shorter loops.** 24-30 s, two sections of 8 or 12 bars, because every rendered minute is
  2.5 MB of history (Size, below). Fifteen minutes is now thirty-odd passes; what carries it is the
  A/B change every 12-15 s and the stems coming and going with the run.

What deliberately did not change: the stem scheme and its thresholds (`Node2DGame`'s music code is
untouched),
the RMS targets (bed -33, pulse -34, lead -35 dBFS - the energy is rhythm, not level), the 80 Hz
and 4.2 kHz master filters, the room, the loop-aware seam machinery, and the shared boss loop,
which is byte-identical to the 2026-10-20 render.

### What a chapter's music is

**Three stems of one loop, plus a boss loop.** `bed`, `pulse` and `lead` are rendered to the
same sample count, tempo and key, and `MusicPlayer` plays them locked together through one
`AudioStreamSynchronized` - the engine's own layered-music stream, so they cannot drift a buffer
apart the way three players started on one frame can. Each stem has a fader:

| Stem | Holds | Up when | Decided in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bed` | held chords, a drone or choir, and the chapter's ostinato | always, while the set plays | `Node2DGame.PlayRunMusic` |
| `pulse` | drums, the driving bass, usually an arpeggio | 28 enemies alive (20% of `MaxEnemies`), out again under 14 | `Node2DGame.UpdateRunMusic` |
| `lead` | the hook in A, its answer in B | an elite alive, or pace minute 10 onward; held 30 real seconds after the elite goes | same |
| boss loop | everything, one file, shared | the boss arrives: 3 s crossfade from the set | `Node2DGame.PlayBossMusic` |
| menu theme | one stem, its own piece | the title and every menu | `MusicPlayer.PlayMenuMusic` |

Layers arrive in 4 s and leave in 8 (a swell should be heard at once; a lull should not become a
gap), on an equal-power curve so a crossfade does not dip 3 dB in the middle. The run fades in
over 3 s while the menu theme fades out over the same 3, everything fades over 2.5 s when the boss
falls or the player dies, and the title brings the theme back over 2. **The menu theme and the
boss loop are both solo loops**, and `MusicPlayer` keeps two solo players so that one can hand to
the other: quitting from a boss fight fades the boss loop out on one while the theme fades in on
the other, where a single player would have had to cut it. Fades run in real time with
`ProcessMode.Always`, so the music keeps moving under a paused level-up.

The pulse and lead thresholds are deliberately on different clocks: *when in the run* the lead
comes in is the pace clock (`PaceMinutes`), *how long it lingers* is real seconds - the rule
`.ai/run-pacing.md` sets for every timing knob.

**Variation lives inside every stem, never as an arc.** A stem with its own build or drop cannot
be faded against the others, so each stem is constant in density and changes colour instead: a
B section changes the ostinato's figure, adds a choir to the bed, and hands the hook to a second
voice. Section-end fills (a tom or tek roll into the next section) are the one exception, and they
come every 12-15 s at the same density, so they are a pattern, not an arc.

### The set

One rule ties it together: **every chapter is a mode of the same seven notes** (A natural
minor's), so every stinger in `sfx.py` fits every chapter, and the mode is what carries the mood.
Only the Emberdeep steps outside, with the boss loop's G sharp and B flat, because it is the end.
`music.py` enforces this now rather than trusting it: `check_scale` refuses to render a note
outside a piece's declared scale, or under E2 (82 Hz), the floor of the frequency budget.

| # | Chapter (boss) | Mode, metre, tempo | Loop | Bed | Pulse | Lead | The wrap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| - | Menu theme | A Aeolian, 4/4, 72 | 8 bars, 26.7 s | one stem: slow strings, drone, harp eighths, a choir in the second half, a heartbeat drum, the horn's theme | - | - | Em to Am |
| 1 | Enchanted Forest (Elderbark) | D Dorian, 6/8, dotted quarter 112 | 24 bars, 25.7 s | strings, drone, a choir in B, spiccato gallop (eighth, two sixteenths, eighth) | harp up-and-back in eighths, plucked bass, frame drums | flute; two horns in octaves in B | Am to Dm, modal v - i |
| 2 | Cursed Dungeon (the Gaoler) | B Locrian over a B drone, 4/4, 132 | 16 bars, 29.1 s | strings, B drone, a low male choir in B, the B-C semitone sawn in sixteenths | taiko in a long room, snare, bassoon on the roots | brass, "da-da DUM" every bar; a chant over brass in B | C to Bdim, the Locrian fall |
| 3 | Sunken Cave (the Hollow Choir) | A Aeolian, 3/4, 160 | 24 bars, 27.0 s | choir forward, strings, low strings rolling up the chord in sixteenth tremolo | deep plucked bass, hand drum and tek, pizzicato in threes across the bar | a wordless solo voice | Em to Am |
| 4 | Blighted Swamp (Mother Rot) | E Phrygian, 7/8 (2+2+3), eighth 280 | 16 bars, 24.0 s | chorused strings, a reed organ pumping each group, beating at 1.6 Hz | plucked bass worrying the E-F half step, dull slack drum, brush | bass flute bending up into each note; a reed in B | F to Em, Phrygian bII - i |
| 5 | Mystic Ruins (the Archivist) | F Lydian, 4/4, 128 | 16 bars, 30.0 s | strings, a choir in B, spiccato in a 3-3-2 tresillo | harp sixteenths, kick, snare, rattle, toms, a soft bell on the off-beats | horn leaping a fourth and a fifth; horn and flute in B | G to F, Lydian II - I |
| 6 | Frozen Waste (the Still Warden) | C Ionian in open fifths, 4/4 at 144 in half time | 16 bars, 26.7 s | glass pad, strings in octaves, root-fifth ticking in eighths - no thirds anywhere | heartbeat taiko (lub-dub), brush on three, sparse plucked bass | a spare flute; the glass shadows it in B | G to C |
| 7 | Scorched Sands (the Long Coil) | G Mixolydian, 6/8, dotted quarter 104 | 24 bars, 27.7 s | a G-D drone fifth, strings, an oud riff in scale degrees from each root | hand drum dum and tek, rattle, plucked bass | shawm, landing on the flat seventh in bar one; paired shawms in B | F to G, bVII - I |
| 8 | The Emberdeep (the Warden of the Deep) | A minor with the Neapolitan B flat and E major, 4/4, 150 | 16 bars, 25.6 s | full choir, strings, a spiccato motor in sixteenths | four-on-the-floor kick, taiko, snare rolls, the boss loop's square bass and pluck | low brass; a chant over brass in B | E to Am, harmonic V - i |
| 9 | The Sketchbook (Wizard Dude) | C major, 3/4, 168 | 24 bars, 25.7 s | soft strings, pizzicato oom-pah-pah | harp eighths, a soft frame drum, brush, a quiet toy tick | music box; a soft flute in B with the music box counting the beats above it | G to C, V - I |

Three things in that table are constraints, not taste:

- **No chapter imitates an effect.** The metal element is an inharmonic ring, the ice element
  inharmonic partials, water a droplet, poison a 9 Hz gurgle, light a bell on G5, arcane two
  detuned triangles at a 17 Hz tremolo. A chapter that borrows one of those constructs puts a fake
  cue under the real one; the prototype boss loop did exactly that (its snare was the metal ring)
  and was fixed. So every struck or plucked voice here is harmonic: the music box is one partial
  with its octave gone in 40 ms, the ruins' bell is partials 1-2-3 decaying in a fifth of a second
  and is never written on G5, the frozen glass is sine, octave and twelfth. The swamp organ beats
  in *amplitude* at 1.6 Hz, not in pitch at 9; the bass flute's bend is 90 cents over 140 ms, not
  a droplet's octave-and-a-half sweep; the tek and the rattle are bands (1.7 and 2.2 kHz), never
  an open highpass. Check a new instrument against the element table in section 4.
- **The Sketchbook is the kids' chapter** and its music respects that the same way the art does:
  nothing in it mocks the drawings, and nothing pretends to be what they drew. It was planned as
  a lullaby and the brief asked for energy, so it is a toy waltz - quick, warm, played straight. A
  music box is a toy that is taken seriously by whoever owns it; that is the register.
- **The Emberdeep is the only chapter allowed outside the seven notes**, and the one that would
  earn its own boss loop first. It runs at 150, faster than the shared boss loop's 138, which is
  deliberate: the finale's descent is the most driven thing in the game, and the fight that ends
  it is a different kind of weight, not more speed.

### The score notation

A chapter's score is written in six helpers, so that it reads as music rather than as tuples:
`line()` for a melody (`"D5:4 A4:2 | F5:4 ..."`, note and length in steps, `.` a rest, and every
`|` a barline that is **checked**, so a bar that does not add up fails at render rather than in the
ear); `held()` for chords held over their run of bars, overlapping the next; `ost()` for an
ostinato, one character per step indexing the bar's chord tones; `riff()` for a figure in scale
degrees from each bar's root (the swamp's bass and the sands' oud follow every chord without
leaving the mode); `seq()` for literal notes that ignore the harmony on purpose (the dungeon's B-C
saw); and `hits()` for drums, `X x o -` for four dynamics. A `Grid` turns (bar, step)
into the piece's beats, which is what lets one notation serve 4/4, 3/4, 6/8 and 7/8.

`--balance` prints each voice's level inside its stem. With nobody able to listen, it is how a
buried part is found: the first render had the cave's tek 23 dB under its stem and the dungeon's
snare 21 dB under, and both were lifted to -13 to -16 before anything was committed.

### The format, and why it differs from the effects

| | Effects | Music |
|---|---|---|
| Rate | 44100 Hz | **22050 Hz, rendered natively** (not downsampled - a filter started from rest at the head of a loop is a click once a cycle) |
| Channels | mono | mono: nothing here is positional, but stereo doubles the weight and buys nothing a synth pad can use |
| Loudness | peak target per file | **RMS target per stem** (`STEM_RMS_DB`), because music is judged by its body, not its loudest sample |
| Fades | 0.4 ms in, 6 ms out | **none** - every file is a loop |
| Import | defaults | `edit/loop_mode=2` (Forward) and `compress/mode=2` (QOA), in each `.import` |

**Loop mode is easy to get wrong.** The importer's enum is *Detect From WAV, Disabled, Forward,
Ping-Pong, Backward*, so **2 is Forward and 1 is Disabled** - and the resulting
`AudioStreamWav.LoopMode` is numbered differently again (0 disabled, 1 forward). It lives in the
`.import` file, so deleting that file loses it. A new track's `.import` can be written *before*
Godot first imports it, with `edit/loop_mode=2` already set; the importer keeps the params it
finds and fills in the uid and path. That is how the 2026-10-22 set went in.
`RegressionChecks.ValidateMusic` warns for any music file that does not loop, for any set whose
stems differ in length, for a chapter in `StageCatalog` with no row in `MusicCatalog.PerStage`,
and for a row naming a chapter that does not exist.

**The file is the mix.** The game plays every stem at unity; the Music slider is the bus.
Levels were set against `mixsim.py --music`, which loops the stems a scenario would have up
under its effects and measures every cast and `player_hurt` against the music beneath it:

| Scenario (tiered policy) | Music up | Music RMS | Under the effects | Median cast over the music (worst tenth) | Median cast over the swarm, without / with music | `player_hurt` over the music |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| early game | bed | -33.2 to -32.8 dBFS | 13.3-13.7 dB | +14.6 to +15.1 dB (+9.3 to +10.4) | +13.1 / +9.9 to +10.6 dB | +19.9 to +23.2 dB |
| early game | bed + pulse | -31.2 to -30.4 dBFS | 10.9-11.7 dB | +12.2 to +13.2 dB (+7.4 to +8.7) | +13.1 / +8.9 to +9.7 dB | +18.4 to +19.9 dB |
| boss | the shared boss loop | -29.7 dBFS | 13.4 dB | +10.1 dB (+3.6) | +5.4 / +3.5 dB | +21.4 dB |
| late game | all three | -29.8 to -28.9 dBFS | 12.9-13.8 dB | +7.9 to +8.7 dB (+3.0 to +4.1) | +3.1 / +1.3 to +1.7 dB | +17.3 to +20.0 dB |

The ranges are across the nine chapters; no chapter is an outlier, which is the point of holding
every one to the same three RMS targets. Against the Forest it replaced, the bed alone measures
the same (its median cast was +14.9, worst tenth +10.0), and the full late-game set costs a cast
the same 1.5 dB or so of its headroom over the swarm; the median late-game cast sits about half a
dB closer to the music (+8.6 then). The new row is bed + pulse, which is where most of a run now
sits, since the pulse is up from 28 enemies: there the music takes 3.4-4.2 dB off a cast's
headroom over a *sparse* swarm, leaving it 9-10 dB clear - more than a late-game cast has with
no music at all.

`player_hurt` stays 17-23 dB over the music in every scenario. The worst critical sound over swarm
and music together is `level_up` at +10.2 dB in the early game (the dungeon, bed + pulse) and
+9.2 dB in the boss fight; in the late game the per-set report names only the worst, and that is
always `elite_spawn` (-6.1 to -8.5 dB), which was already 3.6 dB *under* the late-game swarm before
any music (section 8b) and is a redraw, not a mix problem. Read the late-game row the right way
round: a cast is only 3 dB over the swarm with no music at all, and the music takes 1.5 dB of
that. The swarm is what buries a late cast.

**Turn the music up by raising `STEM_RMS_DB` and re-rendering, not with a `VolumeDb` at a call
site**, and re-run `mixsim.py --music --policy tiered` when you do.

**The budget is enforced, not hoped for.** Every stem passes a 4-pole highpass at 80 Hz and a
4-pole lowpass at 4.2 kHz (`MASTER_HIGHPASS`, `MASTER_LOWPASS`) before its room, so the music
puts nothing in the sub band that belongs to explosions and the boss, and nothing in the 2-5 kHz
band where the element voices live. `analyse.py --music` measures it, on all 28 stems: **0% of
every stem's power is under 80 Hz and 0% above 5 kHz, at most 2% sits in the 2-5 kHz band, and
`hf` is at most 2%.** The beds are 53-80% mid band, the leads 68-100% (the dungeon's brass and the
Emberdeep's are the low end of that). The pulses are the low band's tenants: 19-62% low in the
Sketchbook, forest, ruins and cave, and 78-94% in the sands, swamp, frozen waste, Emberdeep and
dungeon, whose pulse *is* a big drum and a bass - the dungeon's muffled taiko, the frozen
heartbeat. That is about 2 dB more low-band power than the old forest pulse at the same RMS, and
the `player_hurt` column above is the check that it costs nothing that matters: 17-23 dB over the
music everywhere. The first render had the dungeon and Emberdeep pulses at 94-96% low with their
snares 20 dB under the stem; `--balance` found it, the snares and teks came up, and the Emberdeep
pulse gained the boss loop's pluck arpeggio in the mid band.

**Seamless, measured.** `music.py --report` gives three numbers per loop: the sample step at the
wrap against the 99.9th-percentile step in the body, the first-difference energy in a 4 ms window
on the seam against the 99th percentile everywhere else (a click is a burst of exactly that), and
the level of the second around the seam against the loop's median second. Shipped (2026-10-22,
28 files): every step under 0.22 and every click under 0.6 of the loop's own body, and every bed
and pulse within 2.4 dB of its median second at the seam (the frozen bed is the deepest). The
leads read -0.2 to -6.2 dB there because most rest a bar before the wrap, on purpose. Three
things make that true: `render()` folds the overhang of every note past the loop end back onto
the head; chords overlap the next so the last one covers the first one's attack; and every filter
and the reverb run **loop-aware** (`loop_fx`), primed with the end of the loop so they start in
the state the end leaves them in. Without the last one, the reverb is empty at the head of every
cycle.

### Size - read this before re-rendering anything

A minute of mono 16-bit at 22050 Hz is **2.52 MB** and git keeps every version. LFS is off on
purpose (`.gitattributes` says why). The 2026-10-20 Forest was 7.6 MB of stems and the boss loop
1.8 MB. The 2026-10-22 set is 28 files - a 26.7 s menu theme and nine chapters of three 24-30 s
stems - **31.6 MiB (33.1 MB) of WAV**. The three forest files were replaced in place, so their old
7.6 MB stays in history; the boss loop is untouched. All of it went in with one render, and its
blobs compress to about 25.5 MiB in git (loose objects went from 1.05 to 26.8 MiB on staging). In an export QOA carries about 3.2 bits a sample, so the
29 files add about **6.7 MB to the pck** (computed from the format, ~0.2 MB a stem, not measured
from an export).

Every committed re-render of a chapter adds its 3.0-3.8 MB again, and the menu theme its 1.1.
That is why the loops are 24-30 s rather than the forest's old 60, and why this set went in once.

So: iterate with `--scratch` (gitignored) and commit only a track that has been listened to; keep
loops at 30 s or under; share the boss loop until a chapter's fight needs its own; and if the total
starts to bind, a chapter can ship two stems (bed and pulse, the hook moved into the pulse's B
section) before anything is shortened.

### Changing a chapter

Edit its section in `music.py`; render it alone with `--scratch --balance`; check `--report
--scratch`, `analyse.py --music --scratch` and `mixsim.py --music --policy tiered --scratch
--sets <name>`; write the reels with `--journey --scratch` and **listen**; then render it into
`assets/music/` once. A new chapter also needs a `Piece` in `CHAPTERS` (in `StageCatalog` order),
its `.import` files with `edit/loop_mode=2`, and a row in `MusicCatalog.PerStage` -
`ValidateMusic` names any chapter that has none.

### Not yet heard

The 2026-10-22 set was composed, measured and committed on request without anyone listening to it,
which the Don't list below forbids for every later re-render. The first listen will move things:
the knobs are `STEM_RMS_DB` (loudness), the event lists (the music), the velocities `--balance`
reports (the inner mix) and the instrument functions (the timbre). The reels are in
`tools/audio/_music_preview/`: `<chapter>_journey.wav` is the bed alone for one loop, then the
pulse, then the lead, then the boss loop crossfading in, exactly as `MusicPlayer` fades them;
`menu_journey.wav` is the theme twice and a run starting; `all_chapters_sampler.wav` is fourteen
seconds of every piece with everything up, side by side. What to listen for first: whether each
bed's ostinato reads as motion under the chords rather than as clutter; whether the swamp's 7/8
lurches or merely stumbles; whether the music box sits under the effects or pokes through them;
and whether the Emberdeep, faster than the boss loop, makes the fight feel like a drop.

## Don't

- Hand-edit a `.wav` in `assets/sfx/` or `assets/music/`. Edit the builder and re-run.
- Commit a music re-render nobody has listened to. The 2026-10-22 set went in unheard because it
  was asked for; every change to it from here should be heard first. Iterate with `--scratch`;
  every committed re-render is another 1.1-1.3 MB a stem in history.
- Render music pieces in parallel. The machine is shared; one piece at a time.
- Give a music stem its own build or drop. Stems are faded against each other; an arc in one
  cannot be.
- Ship stereo. It costs positional audio and nothing here needs it.
- Fade a loop, or fade anything after normalising.
- Use the module-level `random` anywhere in `tools/audio/`. Seeded instances only, or the
  build stops being reproducible.
- Add a variant file to fix repetition. Randomise `PitchScale` first; variants are a last
  resort and currently exist for exactly one sound.
- Give a swarm-rate sound a sub component, a reverb tail, or a length over ~200 ms.
- Leave noise highpassed with nothing above it, or put `drive()` last in a frequent sound.
  Both are a hiss to Nyquist; see "The ceiling" in section 6.
- Set loudness by how important the event feels. Set it by how often it fires.
- Add a thirteenth element voice without adding its row to `ELEMENTS` and re-running the
  confusion audit.
